channel.description: Recent content in Kanagawa on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Enoshima Aquarium Guide: Tickets, Highlights & Access
item.description: Right on the Shonan coast facing Enoshima island, the Enoshima Aquarium — affectionately known as “Enosui” — is one of the Tokyo area’s most beloved aquariums, blending marine science with a stunning seaside setting. Its star exhibits showcase Sagami Bay, the deep, biodiverse waters just offshore, in a giant tank teeming with sardines, plus a dreamy jellyfish hall, playful dolphin and sea-lion shows staged against a backdrop of the real ocean and Mt.

item.title: Enoshima Guide: Shrine, Sea Candle & Sunset (Kanagawa)
item.description: A small sacred island linked to the Shonan coast by a bridge, Enoshima is one of the most beloved escapes near Tokyo — a hill of shrines, caves, gardens and sea views topped by a lighthouse-like observation tower. Climb (or ride the outdoor escalators) past the Enoshima Shrine to the Sea Candle, whose deck delivers superb panoramas over Sagami Bay to Mt. Fuji, gorgeous at sunset. Below, the wave-carved Iwaya caves and a lively lane of seafood and grilled-octopus stalls make it a perfect half-day, easily paired with the Shonan beaches.

item.title: Hakone Ekiden Guide: New Year Relay Race & Access
item.description: Every January 2nd and 3rd, the nation stops to watch the Hakone Ekiden — the most beloved and dramatic long-distance relay race in Japan. University teams of runners carry a sash (tasuki) over a gruelling ~217 km round-trip course between Tokyo and Hakone, climbing the steep mountain road past Odawara to Lake Ashi and back. The race is a New Year institution, with millions watching on TV and huge crowds lining the route to cheer the young runners through cold, hills and exhaustion.

item.title: Hakone Guide: Mt. Fuji Views, Ropeway & Lake Ashi
item.description: Hakone is the Tokyo area’s favourite mountain getaway — a volcanic resort region of hot springs, lakes and, on clear days, postcard views of Mt. Fuji. The classic experience is the “Hakone loop,” a fun chain of scenic transport: a switchback mountain railway, a cable car, the Hakone Ropeway soaring over the steaming Owakudani valley, and a pirate-ship cruise across Lake Ashi, where Fuji rises beyond a lakeside torii gate. Add world-class onsen, art museums and easy access from Tokyo, and Hakone is one of Japan’s most rewarding day trips or overnight escapes.

item.title: Hakone Onsen Guide: Best Hot Springs, Ryokan & Access
item.description: Hakone is one of Japan’s premier hot-spring (onsen) resorts — a volcanic region where dozens of springs feed historic inns, luxury ryokan and casual day baths, all just over an hour from Tokyo. Soaking in an open-air rotenburo with mountain or valley views, then dining on a multi-course kaiseki dinner in a riverside ryokan, is the quintessential Hakone experience. With more than a dozen distinct onsen towns, mineral waters of every type, and options from budget day-trips to splurge stays, Hakone is the easiest place near the capital to discover Japan’s bathing culture.

item.title: Hakone Open-Air Museum Guide: Tickets, Art & Access
item.description: The Hakone Open-Air Museum was Japan’s first open-air sculpture park, and it remains one of the most delightful art experiences near Tokyo. Set across a sweeping hillside in the Hakone mountains, it scatters more than 100 sculptures by masters like Henry Moore and Niki de Saint Phalle across lawns, gardens and valley views. Highlights include a dedicated Picasso Pavilion, the stained-glass tower Symphonic Sculpture you can climb, playful works kids can clamber on, and a free hot-spring foot bath to soak tired feet.

item.title: Kamakura Festivals Guide: Tsurugaoka Hachimangu & Access
item.description: The ancient samurai capital of Kamakura keeps its warrior heritage alive through a year of vivid festivals centred on Tsurugaoka Hachimangu, the great shrine at the heart of town. The most thrilling is yabusame — mounted archers in full medieval costume galloping down a track, firing arrows at targets — performed at the shrine’s spring and autumn festivals. Around these are portable-shrine processions, traditional dances, the New Year’s first-shrine-visit crowds, and the seaside beach festivals of summer.

item.title: Kamakura Great Buddha Guide: Kotoku-in, Hase & Access
item.description: The serene, weathered Great Buddha of Kamakura (Kamakura Daibutsu) is one of Japan’s most iconic sights — a colossal 13th-century bronze statue of Amida Buddha sitting peacefully in the open air at Kotoku-in temple. Once housed in a great hall that was washed away by a tsunami, the 11.3-metre figure has gazed over the seaside town for some 750 years. Together with the flower-filled Hase-dera temple nearby, it anchors a wonderful half-day in the historic former capital of Kamakura, an easy and rewarding day trip from Tokyo and Yokohama.

item.title: Kamakura Hiking Guide: Daibutsu Trail, Routes & Access
item.description: Beyond its famous temples and Great Buddha, Kamakura hides a network of leafy hiking trails threading through the forested hills that ring the old samurai capital. The best-known, the Daibutsu Trail, links Kita-Kamakura’s temples to the Great Buddha and Zeniarai Benten shrine, while the longer Tenen Trail traces a ridge with sea views. These easy-to-moderate walks let you escape the crowds, pass tucked-away shrines and bamboo, and stitch the town’s highlights together on foot — a refreshing, scenic way to experience Kamakura that combines nature, history and a workout in a single day.

item.title: Kamakura Zazen Guide: Zen Meditation, Temples & Access
item.description: Kamakura is the cradle of Zen Buddhism in Japan — home to the great training monasteries of Kenchoji and Engakuji, founded in the 13th century — which makes it one of the best places for a traveller to try zazen, seated Zen meditation. Several historic temples open their halls to visitors for guided sitting sessions, where you learn the posture, breathing and stillness at the heart of Zen practice, often in a serene hall surrounded by ancient cedars.

item.title: Minato Mirai 21 Guide: Landmark Tower, Views & Access
item.description: Minato Mirai 21 (“Future Port”) is Yokohama’s glittering waterfront district and one of the Tokyo area’s best night-out destinations. Built on reclaimed harbour land, this sleek, futuristic quarter pairs the Landmark Tower — long Japan’s tallest building, with a 69th-floor Sky Garden observatory — with the giant Cosmo Clock 21 Ferris wheel, the historic Red Brick Warehouse, museums, malls and a romantic, illuminated bayfront promenade. Easy to reach and dazzling after dark, it’s the modern face of Yokohama and a perfect complement to the city’s Chinatown and old port heritage.

item.title: Misaki Maguro Guide: Tuna Town, Where to Eat & Access
item.description: At the southern tip of the Miura Peninsula, the fishing port of Misaki is one of Japan’s historic tuna landing harbours — and a paradise for maguro (tuna) lovers. The town built its fame on deep-frozen tuna brought back by long-distance fleets, and today its restaurants serve every part of the fish: glistening maguro-don rice bowls, fatty otoro sashimi, grilled cheeks, simmered collar and even tuna croquettes. Reached by a popular discount “tuna ticket,” Misaki makes a delicious, breezy day trip combining a fishing-town atmosphere, fresh seafood and the wild Miura coast.

item.title: Miura Peninsula Guide: Beaches, Capes & Access
item.description: Jutting into the sea south of Yokohama, the Miura Peninsula is Kanagawa’s breezy coastal escape — a rural finger of land ringed by beaches, fishing ports, sea cliffs and flower fields, all within easy reach of Tokyo. At its tip sits Misaki, a famous tuna port, and the rugged little island of Jogashima with its lighthouse and walking trails. In between are swimming beaches, the science-museum coast of Aburatsubo, seasonal blooms and farm stands piled with Miura’s prized vegetables.

item.title: Mount Oyama Guide: Cable Car, Afuri Shrine & Access
item.description: Rising at the eastern edge of the Tanzawa range, Mount Oyama (1,252 m) has been a place of worship and pilgrimage for centuries — and today it’s one of the most accessible and rewarding half-day mountains near Tokyo. A nostalgic shopping street of tofu restaurants and inns leads to a cable car that climbs to Afuri Shrine, with sweeping views over the Kanto Plain and, on clear days, the sea and Mt.

item.title: Odawara Castle & Hojo Festival Guide: What to See & Access
item.description: The castle town of Odawara, gateway to Hakone, was once the mighty stronghold of the Hojo clan who ruled much of eastern Japan until Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s famous siege in 1590. Today its handsomely reconstructed castle keep anchors a park of cherry trees and museums, and each spring the town celebrates its samurai past with the Hojo Godai Festival, when costumed warriors, princesses and musicians parade through the streets. Add a moat-side bloom of cherry blossoms, a hilltop view to the sea, and the town’s famous kamaboko fish cake, and Odawara makes a rewarding history stop on the way to Hakone.

item.title: Odawara Kamaboko & Seafood Guide: What to Eat & Access
item.description: The castle town of Odawara, gateway to Hakone, is one of Japan’s great homes of kamaboko — the springy steamed fish cake refined here over centuries thanks to fresh Sagami Bay catch and clean mountain water. Beyond the famous pink-and-white loaves, Odawara serves up fresh fish, grilled age-kama fritters, and a lively port market. Visitors can tour kamaboko makers, taste the difference between artisan and everyday versions, and even make their own at hands-on workshops.

item.title: Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum Guide: Tickets & Access
item.description: The Shin-Yokohama Ramen Museum is a food theme park unlike any other — a “ramen amusement park” where you descend into a lovingly recreated 1958 Showa-era streetscape, all flickering neon, retro shopfronts and nostalgic alleys, to slurp your way around Japan’s great regional ramen. Famous shops from Hokkaido to Kyushu (and even overseas) set up here so visitors can taste Sapporo miso, Hakata tonkotsu, Kitakata shoyu and more in one atmospheric basement.

item.title: Shonan Coast Guide: Beaches, Enoden & Access
item.description: The Shonan coast is the Tokyo area’s beloved beach playground — a sunny, laid-back stretch of sand and surf running from Kamakura past Enoshima toward Hiratsuka, all under the gaze of Mt. Fuji on clear days. This is where city-dwellers come to swim, surf, cycle and watch the sunset, riding the charming retro Enoden train as it rattles between the sea and old neighbourhoods. With beaches, Enoshima island, fresh shirasu, and an easygoing California-meets-Japan vibe, Shonan is the perfect seaside complement to historic Kamakura.

item.title: Shonan Shirasu Guide: Whitebait Bowls & Where to Eat
item.description: Along Kanagawa’s Shonan coast, the local delicacy is shirasu — tiny, translucent whitebait (baby sardines and anchovies) landed fresh from Sagami Bay. Served gleaming and raw (nama-shirasu) when the boats are out, or gently boiled (kama-age) and piled over rice, it’s the signature taste of a day at Enoshima and the Shonan beaches. A shirasu-don — a bowl of rice heaped with whitebait, perhaps with an egg yolk and ginger — is the dish to seek out, best enjoyed at a seaside diner with the surf in view.

item.title: Shonan Surfing Guide: Beaches, Lessons & Access
item.description: The Shonan coast is the birthplace and beating heart of Japanese surf culture — a sunny stretch of Sagami Bay where Tokyoites have been riding waves for generations. With gentle beach breaks, a string of surf shops and schools, and Mt. Fuji on the horizon, it’s the most accessible place near the capital to learn to surf or paddle out. Beginners can take a lesson and rent a board on the same beach where locals trade waves at dawn, while the laid-back seaside towns of Kugenuma, Katase and Chigasaki keep the whole scene relaxed and welcoming.

item.title: Tanzawa Mountains Guide: Hiking, Trails & Access
item.description: Rising in western Kanagawa, the Tanzawa Mountains are one of the most popular hiking ranges within easy reach of Tokyo — a green wall of ridges, valleys and waterfalls protected as a quasi-national park. Well-marked trails, mountain huts and ridgeline views (including Mt. Fuji on clear days) draw weekend hikers in every season, from spring greenery and summer escapes from the heat to fiery autumn colours. The signature climb is Mt.

item.title: Yokohama Chinatown Cooking Guide: Classes, Tips & Access
item.description: Japan’s biggest Chinatown, in Yokohama, isn’t just for eating — it’s a great place to learn to cook the very dishes that make it famous. Amid the lantern-hung streets and hundreds of restaurants, cooking studios and classes let visitors get hands-on, folding their own dumplings, shumai and steamed buns, or rolling dim sum under a chef’s guidance, before sitting down to eat what they made. It’s a fun, interactive way to dive deeper into Chinatown than a meal alone, take home a new skill, and understand the Cantonese and regional Chinese cuisine that has thrived in Yokohama since the port opened in the 19th century.

item.title: Yokohama Chinatown Guide: Food, Gates & Access
item.description: Yokohama Chinatown (Chukagai) is the largest Chinatown in Japan — and one of the biggest in the world — a vibrant, lantern-strung warren of some 600 shops and restaurants packed into a few colourful blocks. Marked by ornate paifang gates in every direction, it’s a feast for the senses: steaming dim sum, sizzling street snacks, ornate temples and shops bursting with sweets and souvenirs. Born from Yokohama’s opening as a port in 1859, it’s both a culinary destination and a lively cultural quarter, and an essential stop on any Yokohama visit.

item.title: Yokohama Cosmo World Guide: Ferris Wheel, Rides & Access
item.description: In the heart of Yokohama’s Minato Mirai waterfront, Cosmo World is a compact, colourful amusement park crowned by one of the city’s most recognisable landmarks — the Cosmo Clock 21 Ferris wheel. Once the world’s tallest, this 112-metre giant clock-and-wheel glows in shifting colours after dark and offers a slow, romantic ride over the bay, the skyline and the illuminated harbour. Around it spin roller coasters, a splashy water ride and family attractions.

item.title: Yokohama Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi, Spots & Access
item.description: There are few sights more magical than fireworks (hanabi) bursting over Yokohama’s Minato Mirai skyline, their colours mirrored in the bay beside the glowing Ferris wheel and illuminated towers. Summer is firework season across Japan, and Yokohama’s waterfront — with its open harbour, parks and promenades — makes one of the country’s most photogenic backdrops. From large bay-side festivals to special event displays, tens of thousands gather on warm evenings in yukata to watch the sky light up.

item.title: Yokohama Hakkeijima Sea Paradise Guide: Tickets & Access
item.description: On its own island in Yokohama Bay, Hakkeijima Sea Paradise is a one-of-a-kind resort that fuses a major aquarium complex with an amusement park, shops and restaurants — a full day out for families and couples. Four themed aquariums house some 700 marine species, from whale sharks to penguins, with lively dolphin and sea-lion shows, while thrill-seekers ride a surf coaster that races out over the sea, a tall free-fall tower and a giant Ferris wheel.

item.title: Yokohama Ie-kei Ramen Guide: What It Is & Where to Eat
item.description: Ie-kei (iekei) ramen is Yokohama’s own bold, hearty style of ramen — a rich hybrid of creamy tonkotsu (pork-bone) broth and soy-sauce shoyu, topped with thick straight noodles, big sheets of nori, spinach and chashu pork. Born in Yokohama in the 1970s and named for shops ending in “-ya” (家, “house”), it’s famously customisable: you choose your noodle firmness, broth richness and oil level. Filling, savoury and addictive, it’s a Yokohama institution and the perfect counterpoint to the city’s Chinatown.

item.title: Yokohama Oktoberfest Guide: Beer Festival, Tips & Access
item.description: Each autumn, Yokohama’s historic Red Brick Warehouse (Akarenga) on the waterfront transforms into a slice of Bavaria for the city’s hugely popular Oktoberfest — one of Japan’s largest German beer festivals. Beneath the brick facades and harbour lights, long communal tables fill with revellers raising steins of imported German beer, tucking into sausages, pretzels and roast pork while oompah bands play. With its lively atmosphere, bay-side setting and dozens of beers to sample, Yokohama Oktoberfest is a fun, festive evening out — and the same waterfront hosts spring and other seasonal beer events too.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Kanagawa: Hakone, Yokohama & More
item.description: Kanagawa Prefecture contains two very different travel experiences requiring very different accommodation strategies: Hakone (mountain onsen resort town) and Yokohama/Kamakura (urban coast). Plan which you’re prioritising before booking. Best Areas to Stay Hakone — Japan’s Premier Onsen Resort A mountainous national park 90 minutes from Tokyo by Romancecar express. Staying overnight transforms the experience — day-trippers leave, the mountain mist thickens, and ryokan dinners and private baths become the evening.

item.title: Best Restaurants in Kanagawa: Yokohama, Kamakura & Beyond
item.description: Kanagawa’s food scene is one of the most distinctive in Japan, shaped by the prefecture’s dual identity as an ancient capital and a 19th-century international port. This is the birthplace of Japan’s most copied ramen style, the home of the country’s largest Chinatown, and the region where the Japanese Navy invented curry as we know it. Eating your way through Kanagawa is a journey through modern Japanese food history. Ie-kei Ramen (家系ラーメン) — Yokohama’s Gift to Japan No single city has had more influence on Japanese ramen culture than Yokohama.

item.title: Hakone Complete Guide: Onsen, Art Museums & Mt. Fuji Views
item.description: Hakone is Japan’s most visited onsen resort for good reason: within 90 minutes of Shinjuku, a completely different world opens up. Active volcanoes, a mountain lake reflecting Mt. Fuji, outdoor sculpture gardens, and hundreds of ryokan offering hot spring baths with mountain views. The challenge isn’t finding things to do — it’s choosing between them. This guide breaks down every decision you’ll need to make. Choosing Your Base: The 17 Onsen Areas Hakone comprises 17 separate onsen resort areas (温泉地), each with a distinct character and elevation.

item.title: Kanagawa Family Trip: Best Activities & Sights for Kids
item.description: Kanagawa is one of Japan’s finest prefectures for families: there are pirate ships, volcano steam vents, giant Buddhas you can climb inside, an aquarium where you can touch starfish, and a museum dedicated entirely to instant noodles. This guide covers the best family-friendly experiences across Kamakura, Yokohama, Hakone, and Enoshima — with practical notes on transport, timing, and what ages enjoy each activity most. 🏴‍☠️ Hakone: The Family Adventure Hub Hakone Pirate Ship (芦ノ湖遊覧船) The Lake Ashi sightseeing boats — styled as European galleons complete with cannons, masts, and pirate flags — are one of Japan’s most memorable transport experiences for children.

item.title: Kanagawa Girls' Trip: Kamakura, Yokohama & Hakone for Women
item.description: Kanagawa offers a girls' trip that Tokyo simply cannot match: the intimacy of Kamakura’s temple lanes, the refined European atmosphere of Yokohama’s Yamate bluff, a ryokan night in Hakone with private outdoor baths, and the Enoshima love rituals that make Japan’s shrine culture genuinely romantic. This guide covers the best experiences for groups of women across the prefecture. 👘 Kimono Experience in Kamakura Kamakura is arguably Japan’s finest kimono destination outside of Kyoto — the combination of temple approaches, stone-paved lanes, and bamboo groves creates photography backgrounds impossible to replicate elsewhere.

item.title: Kanagawa Goshuin Guide: Temple & Shrine Stamp Routes
item.description: Kanagawa contains some of Japan’s most historically significant goshuin destinations — Kamakura alone was the seat of Japan’s first shogunate and is home to over 65 temples and shrines within walking distance of each other. Unlike Kyoto’s well-trodden pilgrimage circuits, Kamakura’s goshuin routes remain genuinely quiet on weekday mornings, and several sites — Kakuon-ji cave shrine, Engaku-ji’s inner precinct, Hokoku-ji bamboo grove — are rarely crowded regardless of season. 御朱印とは？ — What is Goshuin?

item.title: Kanagawa Hidden Gems: Beyond Kamakura, Yokohama & Hakone
item.description: Kanagawa is one of Japan’s most visited prefectures — yet the vast majority of foreign tourists funnel through the same circuit: Kamakura Great Buddha, Hakone hot springs, Yokohama Chinatown. What they miss is extraordinary. A southernmost Pacific cape where seabirds nest in basalt cliffs. A village that serves as the Emperor’s private retreat. A Zen temple in a bamboo valley accessible only by guided tour, where 13th-century stone Buddhas have never been moved.

item.title: Kanagawa Honeymoon Guide: Romantic Stays, Private Onsen & Scenic Moments
item.description: Kanagawa may be the most complete honeymoon destination in Japan: it offers Hakone’s private volcanic onsen with Mt. Fuji views, the refined European atmosphere of Yokohama’s bluff district, Kamakura’s ancient shrine lanes at dusk, and the Enoshima love rituals at Japan’s most romantic island. All of this is within 90 minutes of Tokyo — ideal for couples combining a city stay with a quieter, more intimate escape. ♨️ The Ryokan Night: Hakone’s Private Onsen A night in a Hakone ryokan with a private outdoor bath (rotenburo) attached to the room is the defining romantic experience of Kanagawa — and one of the finest in Japan.

item.title: Kanagawa Mystery & Puzzle Guide: Escape Rooms, Treasure Hunts & Hidden History
item.description: Kanagawa offers a different kind of puzzle experience from Tokyo — where Tokyo’s escape rooms are theatrical productions, Kanagawa’s best mystery experiences are embedded in the landscape itself: the medieval street grid of Kamakura hides genuine historical puzzles, Hakone’s old mountain roads are layered with centuries of strategic history, and Yokohama’s foreign settlement district holds architectural mysteries from the Meiji era. This guide covers both the organised puzzle venues and the self-discoverable mystery experiences across the prefecture.

item.title: Kanagawa Nature Guide: Hakone Volcanoes, Kamakura Trails & Shonan Coast
item.description: Kanagawa contains more ecological variety than any other prefecture near Tokyo. Within 90 minutes of Shinjuku you can stand inside an active volcanic crater, hike a mountain ridge used by samurai armies, surf a Pacific beach, or kayak among sea caves on a wild volcanic cape. The prefecture is almost entirely overlooked by nature travellers who default to the Japanese Alps — a significant mistake. Hakone: Volcanic Landscape and Mountain Drama Owakudani — Japan’s Most Accessible Active Volcano Owakudani (大涌谷, “Great Boiling Valley”) is a volcanic caldera created by the eruption of Mt.

item.title: Kanagawa Solo Travel Guide: Hiking, Ramen, and Japan's Most Rewarding Day Trips
item.description: Kanagawa is ideal for solo travel: it is safe, well-signed in English, has excellent public transport, and offers experiences that are actually better alone — the Kamakura hiking trails are meditative at your own pace, Hakone is most efficient as a solo day trip, and Yokohama’s Noge bar district is one of the few places in Japan where solo travellers are welcomed at the bar counter as a matter of course.

item.title: Top 20 Sightseeing Spots in Kanagawa: Kamakura, Yokohama & Hakone
item.description: Kanagawa prefecture packs more variety into a single train journey than almost any region in Japan. Within 90 minutes of Tokyo you can stand before a 13-metre bronze Buddha, gaze across a sulphur-smoking volcanic crater toward Mt. Fuji, or wander a Meiji-era harbour district that looks like it belongs in Shanghai. This guide ranks the top 20 spots — including several hidden corners that even regular Japan visitors miss entirely.
